recall_prompt: Say how you would find the middle term — how the parity of n decides how many there are and which one, and what the term comes to with its sign.
insider_note: n = 10 is even, so there is ONE middle term, the 6th. (−2y)⁵ keeps its minus — an odd power preserves the sign, and a positive final term shows it was dropped.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Decide which term is the middle
steps.margin_note: First mark. n = 10 is even, so there is ONE middle term, the (n/2 + 1)-th = 6th.
lines: n = 10 is even, so there is one middle term,

recall.must_convey: That n = 10 is even so the single middle term is the 6th, T₆ = ¹⁰C₅ (3x/7)⁵ (−2y)⁵.
accept: n is ten which is even so the middle term is the sixth, ten C five into three x by seven to the five into minus two y to the five
even n gives one middle term, n by two plus one which is six
T six is ten C five three x by seven power five minus two y power five
n ten even kabatti one middle term, sixth term
the middle term of an even power is the n by two plus one th

steps.why: An expansion with n + 1 terms has a single middle only when n + 1 is odd, that is when n is even; it is then the (n/2 + 1)-th term.
common_mistakes: Taking the 5th term as the middle.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.margin_note: Second mark. (−2y)⁵ = −2⁵y⁵ — an odd power keeps the minus. (3/7)⁵ · 2⁵ = (6/7)⁵.

recall.must_convey: That the middle term is −¹⁰C₅ (6/7)⁵ x⁵y⁵, negative because the power 5 is odd.
accept: minus ten C five into six by seven to the five x to the five y to the five
the sign is negative because minus two y is raised to an odd power
three by seven to the five times two to the five is six by seven to the five
minus ten C five six by seven power five x power five y power five

steps.why: (−2)⁵ is negative and 3⁵·2⁵ = 6⁵, so the two constants collapse into one fraction to the fifth power.
common_mistakes: Leaving (3/7)⁵ · 2⁵ uncombined when the paper expects (6/7)⁵.
